title: Alauddin Fixes the Price of Wheat

title_i18n.en: Alauddin Fixes the Price of Wheat

subtitle: How Siege and Suspicion Built Alauddin’s Iron Market in Delhi
region: Delhi, Siri and the grain routes of the Doab
moral: Order can feed a city, but coercion has a cost.

sources.citation: Ziauddin Barani, Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, account of Alauddin's market regulations
sources.note: Most detailed source for fixed prices, spies, granaries and punishments.
Contemporary court account giving a more benevolent explanation.

sources.citation: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals, Part I (2007)
sources.note: Modern university-level synthesis of the reforms and their purposes.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of throne hall

dialogue.text: In the anxious years after Mongol sieges, Sultan Alauddin Khalji remade Delhi’s markets with iron rules so a hungry capital and vast army could eat at fixed, cheap prices.
Delhi had tasted fear. After sieges and Mongol alarms, grain thinned, prices rose, and hunger stared from the lanes of the Sultan’s proud capital.
Alauddin had fought hard to hold Hindustan, always watching the Mongol steppe beyond the passes. To keep a great standing army, he needed grain and cloth, horses and men, at costs he could command.
Barani, writing later, tells us the Sultan feared two things: nobles growing too rich to rebel, and merchants pushing up prices so every soldier’s ration drained the treasury.

dialogue.speaker: alauddin_khalji
dialogue.text: Delhi shall not starve at a merchant’s whim. We will fix the price of wheat.
From the grain fields of the Ganga–Yamuna Doab to the mandis of Delhi, the Sultan’s order spread. The state would watch every route where wheat and rice rolled into the city.

He set schedules of rates—grain, cloth, animals, slaves, and daily goods. It was among the most systematic state market interventions seen in medieval India, built on fear, calculation, and a desire for order.
In the grain markets, officials checked weights, measured heaps, and enforced the Sultan’s rates. Traders could no longer hoard in secret or raise prices with the season’s turn.
Barani speaks of the Sera-i-Adl, where justice met trade. Here, the Sultan’s agents watched over buying and selling, a state shadow cast across every bargain.
The Sultan filled granaries with harvests drawn from the countryside. When scarcity threatened, the state could release grain, steadying prices and feeding barracks and alleys alike.
He relied on state carriers to move food and cloth from field to city. The path of each cart now lay under the Sultan’s gaze, not just under village bargains.
Barid spies slipped through shops and serais, listening. A secret note, a whispered complaint, could reach the court by nightfall. Suspicion became part of the market’s air.
Barani’s pages tell of harsh punishments for those who broke the rules—hoarders, false measurers, secret dealers. The Sultan believed fear would hold prices down where trust could not.
Amir Khusrau saw welfare in this order: the poor could buy food, soldiers were fed, chaos stilled. Yet many merchants felt crushed, their profit clipped by an iron hand.

dialogue.speaker: alauddin_khalji
dialogue.text: An empire stands not only on steel, but on full stomachs.
With fixed prices, the state could maintain vast forces at lower cost. Mongol threats still loomed, but Delhi’s barracks now had steady rations, and the treasury breathed easier.
For years, Alauddin’s regulations held. Grain, cloth, and cattle moved under rules, and every deal in Delhi knew the Sultan’s silent presence beside the scales.
After Alauddin’s death in 1316, his system was swiftly dismantled. The speed of its undoing suggests the relief of merchants and nobles who had long chafed under his strict controls.
Alauddin’s market reforms stand as a warning and a lesson: state power can feed a city and armies through order, but when fear rules every bargain, the cost is borne in silence and resentment.
